utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As you see Judge Janu couldn't be with us today because she is not feeling well and I have provisionally released her from her responsibilities today. It's only something temporary which should only last today. We shouldn't really be worried about it. But I am going to apply the Rules and we are going to sit with two judges. It shouldn't be a problem with anyone, I suppose. So, Mr. Brdjanin, have you understood what I said? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are understanding and you are hearing in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin as case manager today. I was about to remark, Your Honour, that I appear to have the most appalling affect on my cases because in the Stakic case we had the same problem, although rather more serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is only something very temporary and we shouldn't be worried about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I happened to look very closely at Rules so, Your Honour is quite right. Your Honour can carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan Trbojevic, attorney. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And assisted by Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you both. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have the waiver for today's sitting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So any preliminaries? I hope not. Mr. Usher, please, the witness. And let's hope we can send him back to somewhere where it's more sunny -- where it's sunny, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I invite you to make your solemn declaration once more before we proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Mr. Zecevic for General Talic will be continuing with his cross-examination of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Filipovic, please allow a brief interval between question and answer and answer and question, so as not to render the interpreters' life more difficult than it already is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. May the usher please put on the ELMO the map P446.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, yesterday we broke speaking about the weapons. Do you remember? Could you tell me, Mr. Filipovic, do you know the Hukanovic brothers, Arif and Ferid from Vrhpolje, municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of them but I don't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the two of them brought weapons to the territory of the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that personally. I've heard some rumours but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday, you explained what the organisation of the Territorial Defence was. Could you perhaps confirm that the Territorial Defence was organised according to the territorial principle?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of Bosanski Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that there were 12 companies in that territory, in that area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Fewer than 12?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, officially, we had only one official formation that was in Velagici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, is it true that some meetings due to the secrecy that we spoke about, that they were held in mosques?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. We had to hold them because we didn't have room to hold them elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a hodza from Vrhpolje, an Emir Seferovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in contact with the Crisis Staff that was formed in Vrhpolje?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I said that I was only personally in contact with Dr. Nezim Mutic from Prijedor and with Mr. Karabeg because we are friends, close friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, do you know Mr. Muhamed Posovljak [phoen]. He was a hodza in Krasulje?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he's Muhamed. I think it's Muharem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Muharem Posovljak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as an acquaintance. I know he was a hodza in Krasulje. I know that when he was in the Manjaca camp, he didn't behave well towards me so I don't have a high opinion of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps or perhaps you've heard later on that Mr. Posovljak was a hodza from Krasulje. Following the ambush in Krasulje he negotiated with your late brother and Mr. Kondic; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. That was at the time when I was already imprisoned on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me about some actual events from the 26th of May onwards?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1992. On several occasions during your yesterday's testimony, and during your testimony in examination-in-chief, you said that your main objective in establishing the Patriotic League and the Territorial Defence was the Defence itself.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that sense, you establish -- because of that, you established the staff which was in Pudin Han in the Dom Kulture, in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it was to this purpose that there was some trenches that were dug; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's not correct. Because Kljuc is a town where there have been trenches since Second World War so if there are trenches, there are trenches from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the trenches in the area of Velagici, Krasulje, Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May well be. When there was the incident on the 27th, but before that, as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you are making the plans for the defence, did you also have a -- the route from withdrawal, route for direction for retreat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we had. In our plans, we had planned to somehow establish a contact with Sanski Most and then if it was possible to have a link to Bihac, communication with Bihac because we knew that there was no hope to go towards Banja Luka or Zenica or Sarajevo, because most of the population of our ethnicity were in the Bihac area, in the Bihac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that this route via Vrhpolje towards Bihac, Sanski Most, so towards Bihac, this route was at the end of the day after all these events, this is where the units of Omer Gromilic and Avdo Ceric went; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, you had a plan and in that plan, that a collection point for withdrawal was the village of Krasulje towards Vrhpolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is about midway of that part of the Kljuc municipality, which allowed for the possibility for all the citizens to come, all the locals to come, because it's roughly the centre of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to indicate for us on this map, 446, if you can just indicate where Krasulje is, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me, so you also had a field hospital, so it to speak, prepared in Hedipoci [phoen]. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a hospital, because we didn't have any equipment, so you can't really say that we had a field hospital. If anyone had any bandages in their possession, but because we all had been in the JNA so we had the first aid kit and that's where the bandages came from. That's the only thing that we had in terms of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you also had a plan to evacuate civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well of course, that would be logical, if the army is withdrawing, of course the population would withdraw as well, together with the soldiers, because troops, that is the Territorial Defence, is defending the civilian population. It's not defending itself. It's defending the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that on Tuesday, 26th of May, 1992, eight soldiers came to be imprisoned in the village of Srlinje [phoen], you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was 25th of May. 25th or 26th, but more probably it was 25th. I don't know what the number was. I think I said that in my testimony, and my late brother ordered that they should not be harmed, that they had to stay alive, which did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony you told us that you were informed about this by Atif Dedic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Atif Dedic, if I remember correctly, your testimony, he was a policeman in Kljuc; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this unit in Srlinje was commanded by Eso Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander but I do know Eso and I know that with Atif together they did -- they informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, Eso Osmanovic was from the village of Srlinje?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and so was Atif Dedic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So these soldiers were imprisoned or were captured and your late brother issued instructions that they should not be harmed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is all that more or less happened on that 26th when you found out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except that my brother said that they should be locked up somewhere and then these two said people are very angry, upset, we have IDed them, they are from Kragujevac, they are from Serbia, from Kragujevac, but Omer said that they should be taken to the best house with the best cellar. That's where they should be put, with the most responsible house with the most responsible people who should guard them and nobody should harm them. So they stayed there. I don't know what their further fate was, although I did find out in Manjaca that they stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me, do you know if your late brother managed to establish a contact with the authorities, either military or civilian authorities in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my brother went to Velagici after that incident. He said -- I stayed in Kljuc. My wife and his wife remained, but my brother said what we feared most has just begun. And the wife started to cry and we were very upset as well because we knew what the -- what war meant. Although we hadn't lived through a war, we knew that this was, the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've understood you correctly. Your brother, after these eight soldiers were captured in the village of Srlinje, they were imprisoned by the unit from the village of Srlinje which had at least 30 members?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many members it had, but these were locals. These were local people mostly, all from Srlinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that occasion, there were no clashes of any kind between the troops?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no operations there at all, because the reservists from the JNA from Kragujevac, they entered an ambush and they said later on that they had been sent to reconnaissance. Well, you can imagine where Kragujevac is, where Serbia is. They didn't know the field, they didn't know the terrain, so they just walked into the ambush by our boys. But as far as I know, not a shot was fired. There was no fighting of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of this, I'm asking you how come that your late brother said, "What I feared most happened"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? The war. The war was starting. The war was starting. Sometimes it starts with a bullet being fired and sometimes it starts with the murder of the Austro-Hungarian heir to the thrown. And here it started that we were so -- we should be so naive and daft as to kill eight JNA soldiers. We always tried not to do this and I always said and it was true that we prepared ourselves for the defence. We did not want to kill them, and we didn't do it. Omer went to the command in Velagici and whether he had any telephone contact with Vinko Jovo, I don't know. That was 5 kilometres away from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The next morning, early, there was a barricade that was set up on the main road near the Krasulje village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it later. I wasn't an eyewitness. I wasn't there but I was told about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And since we heard all about all this so that we shouldn't go into detail, but the police set off and one unit that was commanded by Aziz Gromilic fired and killed deputy of the -- deputy chief of the police station, killed Dusan Stojkovic and wounded some policemen. You heard about it later?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about it later. That's what the rumours were. I have my own personal opinion. I believe that this was not -- these were not -- shots were not fired from the positions of the Territorial Defence of the Bosnian Kljuc Territorial Defence because the last few days before that, the Serb authorities insisted to create an incident so that a clash, conflict, would appear. Of course, the Chamber doesn't have to believe me. This is my opinion. Of course, there has been no investigation to find out from which side Dusan Stojkovic was fired at, so it may have happened that he was fired from the back by his own colleagues, because there was no investigation that was conducted. And it is true that Dusan Stojkovic was killed and Milos Kecman was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You certainly heard that your late brother went to intervene precisely because the police wanted to conduct the investigation. This was not possible because of the resistance proffered by the Territorial Defence unit commanded by Aziz Gromilic, and in fact they waited in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They insisted to come but they didn't want to do an investigation. They wanted to take the body of Dusan Stojkovic. And these boys, these men from Krasulje said, "We will only let you come if Vinko comes and if Omer comes." And then Vinko got in touch with Omer. And I found about -- found out about that and because our telephone lines were cut, I was called at home, and he said I had to go and this is when we agreed that I should watch the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That ambush in Krasulje was around -- it was in the morning, around 10.00. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly what time it was because it was still a working day, on the 27th people still worked. But I know that about around noon, in the municipality where I had a job, although nothing had been done for the last month, I went out on my own initiative but later on I found out that around -- in the afternoon, all the Muslims and Croats had just been thrown out of the municipality building in Kljuc. They were told that they were Ustashas, that they were balijas. They said, "We don't need you here." These were people who had been colleagues of ours until the other day, lawyers, et cetera who had worked with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, please let's try to concentrate on the question.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question is about the ambush at 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when the people were thrown out then, and they were thrown out around noon, I think that around that time, it happened, whether it was at 10.00 or 10.15, I don't know, but it was around that time. I'm trying to answer your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you know that around noon, fire was opened at a police checkpoint in Velagici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Fadil Pobric?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Maybe if I saw him because there are various names in our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He had a light machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, but we should know who his father was because there are four Filipovic Muhameds in Kljuc, so if you don't tell me who his father is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At 1400 hours on that very same day, there was a military convoy in Pudin Han which was ambushed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. I was told it was on the 27th but again, I don't know when it was exactly because at that time there was shooting in Kljuc from all directions. They even shot from directions where the Green Berets and Territorial Defence couldn't have shot from, from the direction of Rajkovi. That's where fire came from. So that can't be under Muslims and -- a Muslim couldn't have shot from there. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that ambush, after the military convoy was ambushed, do you know that at the time, six soldiers were killed and 25 were seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard when I got to the prison in Stari Gradiska. I didn't know that up until that point, but when the soldier was reporting to the captain, that's when I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after that event that took place at 1400 hours on the 27th of May, 1992, the Territorial Defence units blocked the road from Laniste to Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I assume that that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that part of the plan that we have discussed, your defence plan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not far from Laniste there is a part of the Kljuc municipality. It's only a kilometre or two away. And in that area, in military terms, creating an obstruction would be the safest thing for all those structures that are being defended, that would be the safest place, the best place, to establish an obstruction, you're -- on the territory of your municipality. We didn't enter the municipality of Petrovac. We didn't enter that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That same day, on that same day, at around 2000 hours in the evening, 80 kilos of explosives were planted on that same road. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard this -- I've just heard this now from you, because I personally don't think that we had 80 kilos of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Zukic Faik who activated those explosives at 5.00 in the morning on the next day, on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I've heard about this. The first time I've heard that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I have a slight qualification about this cross-examination. At the moment, Mr. Zecevic is asserting a number of things as facts which have not been put in evidence and the witness is being made to believe there is evidence to this effect. I think Mr. Zecevic should rephrase the question slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner is correct, Mr. Zecevic. I know that you haven't come to your stage of bringing forward evidence, of course, but both Ms. Korner and myself come from a jurisdiction where what she has just pointed out is the practice. And I think it ought to be the practice because no witness should be presented with a fact as if this has already been established before this Tribunal or evidence brought forward, et cetera. So in other words, what you need to do is you put it to the question -- to the witness in a way as to ask him whether he has any information or whether he is aware of -- but without making it appear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, tell me, in addition to all of this that I have mentioned, the outline of the events in those three -- during those three days from the 26th to the 28th of May, when you were arrested in 1992, do you stand by the claim that on that occasion, the Territorial Defence units were defending themselves?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that this wasn't a plan, an attack, a plan for an attack that had been prepared in advance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We knew that if that had happened on our side, if the convoy had been fired at -- well we didn't know that the convoy was going to appear. And secondly, since the situation was as it was, the other side, the Serbian side, should have tried to clarify things in political terms. They shouldn't have sent people to their death. So Vinko Kondic and Jovo Banjac should have said, "Listen people, it's a crisis. Let's sit down and try to reach an agreement." But according to information that I had, they sent Dusan Stojkovic and Milos Kecman, who got out of the car in an aggressive manner. They verbally attacked people. They cursed their Turkish mothers, they said, "What do you Turks want?" That's what people say. I wasn't there, but I'm just telling you what people in Manjaca told me. And it is my personal opinion that that would have been possible if war was to be avoided, then a political meeting should have been held to attempt to do this, to avoid war. So if there hadn't been any defence from the direction of Brescica -- Ravko Boric [phoen] and Marko Adamovic commanded these units. They were deployed and fired at Velagici. People had to defend themselves. So it was pure defence. So I stand by the claim that we defended ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've already spoken about this in the course of the examination-in-chief, but there is just one other thing. When you speak about this ambush in Krasulje when Dusan Stojkovic and Milos were killed, you said that they irritated because they got out of the car in an aggressive manner. Would it be true to say that the ambush had already been laid there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- Mr. Zecevic, the men were at their positions, but I can claim for sure that none of our men had the intention to do anything, to take any action. But would you allow me to enter your house in Belgrade, which is where you're from, and allow me to steal things, to rape? You have to defend yourselves. If there is no system to defend you, you have to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you know that on those same days, from the 25th of May to the 27th of May, in the territory of Prijedor municipality and in the territory of the -- of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje too, there were also defensive actions carried out by the BH Territorial Defence as you say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you have followed the situation in Bosnia in 1992, if you followed the situation, everything took place within two days. In Kljuc it began on the 27th. Two days before, it was in Sana and two days before Sana, there was Prijedor. So on the basis of this analogy, if we look back into the past, it's not possible to say that people provoked conflicts but the JNA that had been organised went from place to place and I'm talking in military terms. If at the same time -- if they had attacked the Bosnia-Herzegovina, all of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the same time, things would have been different, because people were under the impression they are going to attack Prijedor and the people in Sana said, "They are not going to attack us. They will stop in Prijedor." I have such experience in Kljuc. When they came to Sanski Most, they said, "Well, let it be, they will stop in Sana and nothing will happen in Kljuc." And then two days later, the same thing happened in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, wouldn't it be true to say that there was a coordinated action in the territory of Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the objective of this action was to cut offer the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's not true. I know that we in Kljuc worked on an independent basis and therefore, if it had been coordinated, we would have made a move on the same -- on the same day when Kozarac and Prijedor were attacked. So there was no coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to show us on this map, 446, could you show us the following places, Kozarac, Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, and Velagici down below. Kozarac, first, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you can't find it on the map point to somewhere nearby?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the immediate vicinity of Prijedor. A few kilometres from Prijedor, you know. So next to Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... recognise the names on this map? Thank you. So Kozarac is -- yeah --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you now show us where Vrhpolje and Hrustovo are located in the territory of Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in on to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, these are two villages which up until 1962, were in the municipality of Kljuc, and from 1962 onwards they became part of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And finally Velagici, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velagici. Could you zoom in? Velagici is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the technician please zoom out a bit so we can see the whole map, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would agree that the line which would connect these three places or the four places that you have indicated, really passes through the middle and cuts through Bosnian Krajina, it separates it into two parts, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Geographically, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown DT-30, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, this is a magnified photocopy of your brother's signature. We think that this is your brother's signature. Could you perhaps confirm this for us?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it should be his signature, that it is his signature. But this letter here, it was a bit bigger when he signed, but I don't know under what conditions he signed this, but this letter "O" was always as big as the "V."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you allow for the possibility that this could be your brother's signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know under what conditions he signed this, but this is his signature but the letter "O" should be a little bigger, because my signature is such that anyone could read it, but it's easy for me to recognise my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, please, P90? And Mr. Usher, what I would like you to do is put DT-30 on the ELMO and this document which the witness is actually inspecting right now. Both of them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, this is an official report from the MBO and the SDA in Kljuc dated the 31st of October, 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read it correctly, but -- I haven't read it well, but it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the signature of your late brother, which is at the back of the document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as I said, have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to put both documents there and to indicate to us what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see the letter "V" and the letter "O" here in his signature. They are more or less the same size. You can't measure it this in millimetres but it should be more or less the same size but here, the "V" is bigger than the "V" here, but I still think that this is his signature. It depends on how -- whether he was in a hurry when he signed, but I would just comment on the letter "O" because if you -- I would object to the letter "O" because if you compare it with the signature here, you can see that the letter "V" is about the same size as the letter "O."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, please, DT31?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the statement of the late Omer Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately the translation is not available. As soon as we got it on the 26th of August, we gave it and unfortunately I don't have a translation as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd ask that we be provided with a translation before documents are being put in, if that's possible or a summary. We try at least to do a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours we have given the document as soon as we found the document when we came over here on the 26th of August, and it is with the ICLC and its translation is still pending, as far as I'm aware of. And we called them and the Registry and asked them many times that this be provided if possible, but unfortunately, until today, we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, in the first break, in the course of the first break, could you check with the department concerned to see what has happened to this document? And in any case, irrespective of whether they have translated it or not, signal the importance and the need to have it translated by next Monday at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have the interpreters been provided a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, have you seen this statement before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've seen it, and as I said earlier on, it depends under what conditions he signed. So the circumstances of the investigation while he was in prison, and you would agree with me that in such cases, something changes in a man so perhaps his signature changed too. That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the last page, the date is the 29th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. The 29th of May, 1992, in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, since we don't have the translation, we will have to go through this statement very briefly and I'm going to read certain parts out to you. On page 4, the third paragraph, "In the area of the town centre in which the population is mixed, Muslim and Serb, we did not have any units that had been formed, because there were no conditions for them to take action. But in suburb and settlements we had formed two companies, for the Sehici settlement, one company with the commander Rifat Sehic, who had been elected by soldiers from that company. The second company was for the Rejzovici settlement, for Mali Rejzovici settlement and for the Egrlici settlement. The commander of this company was Ibrahim Egrlic, a reserve captain. "In the territory of the Velagici local commune, we had three companies. Djeric Nevzet, a reserve colonel was -- had the duty of organising these companies. In cooperation with soldiers he worked on electing and appointing a company commander. The exact deployment of the commanders, according to -- in the units, is something that I do not know. I know that from the 27th of May of this year, Avdic Amir, in brackets, who worked on the formation of the units for the Biljani area, Salihovic Salih, and Ceman Fahrudin, who had a high political post, worked directly with me or they contacted me through the intermediary of someone else. I can't remember any other names and I don't know the platoon commanders. "For the Biljani area, as I have already said, Avdic Amir was responsible for this area. But just before the conflict began on the 27th of May, he moved over to Vojici from Biljani, a few days prior to this date. And he is married in Vojici. Ale Mujezinovic was made responsible for Biljani but not by me. And he formed three companies in this area. I don't know the names of any other commanders. Ale Mujezinovic may be the commander of one company." I'm not going to read out what it says about the Sanica settlement but in the following paragraph, "In the area of Krasulje, which belongs to the local commune of Peci, and given how we have organised this, it is in fact an independent local commune, the organisation of one fortified company in terms of numbers, not in terms of materiel and equipment which consisted of about 150 people, was led and organised by Ismet Muratagic. I don't know the officers subordinated to him." What I have just read is contained in the statement, isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but before all this, when you asked about that meeting yesterday, I said that if we had had all of this at our disposal, the sixth American fleet wouldn't have been necessary for us. What has been said about Krasulje is okay, is correct, but not about Biljani. What was said about Velagici is correct, and I continue to claim that there were people who joined up in Krasulje and in Velagici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Further on in the statement, as you will see, Mr. Filipovic, your late brother further speaks about other villages and local communes where there were also units, like the local commune of Humici, settlement of Srlinje, settlement of Laniste, local commune of Kamecak [phoen] and so on. On page 6, so that we don't waste much time, the very last paragraph on page 6, "According to my assessment, one could count or at least I counted on composition of 1200 to 1300 people. As for the weapons, I believe that not all men were armed. I think that we had at our disposal about 800 guns, pieces of different types. Mostly these were hunting weapons with permits, pistols or handguns with permits, while as far as the non-registered weapons were concerned, these were mostly automatic and semi-automatic rifles. I cannot comment on the number of automatic rifles. We had some M-53 light machine-guns. I saw one army sniper, when one of the soldiers brought it to the cultural centre and asked Djeric to explain something to him. We had at our disposal one mortar, 60 millimetre mortar. We had one hand-held launcher, and up to ten rocket -- hand-held rocket launchers. The position of mortar was in the area of Vojici"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should read how many shells we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we are all at a loss now, if that is in the document that the witness has just referred to, then it ought to be read to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it in the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, but he's just said you should read the shells. Now I have no way of reading the shells because there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you know the document, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't. Is there mention of the amount of shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honour, but I'm conducting the cross-examination and not the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if the witness says, "I could have a whole arsenal of weapons, but if I don't have any ammunition, I can't use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The difficulty is absolutely right. I could re-examine if that was possible but it isn't. And if a witness actually says, "Read on." Normally I would stand up and say you should read the next sentence because I'm able to see what the next sentence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No problem. I should read the next sentence as well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Any way, I mean let's not make an incident out of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know where the relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Points out, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, not just to let you worry about this, you will of course have the opportunity to re-examine the witness as soon as Mr. Zecevic finishes. However, if on the basis of this, the incognito element of this document, you feel uncomfortable about concluding your re-examination, I can reserve you the right to bring back Mr. Filipovic if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would hope, Your Honour, that won't be, but if necessary, until I see a full translation of this document -- I haven't the faintest idea what's in it, and I think I'm going to say in future, I should, I'm afraid with everything that happened, I didn't appreciate that we had an untranslated document given to us. I'm going to object to documents being put in unless we are provided with some kind of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, I mean they submitted it way back in August. So it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A month now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, they have their own -- it's perfectly possible to provide at least a summary or a translation themselves of what parts are going to be put, but anyhow Your Honour I'm just saying that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just address this, Your Honour. We have provided the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution with -- we disclosed the copy of this statement at the same time when we gave it to the translators, so on the August 26th. Since the Prosecutor's Office has means and the whole staff of translators, I would assume that you will have the, at least the summary or an unofficial translation, because according to the practice of this Tribunal, we are not allowed to have our translations but we have to apply to the CLSS. Thank you. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We had at our disposal four mortar shells, that, according to what I learned, were not used. The position of the rocket launcher -- not the -- the RB, the hand-held rocket launcher, I cannot tell you about because I didn't decide on its use, but I don't think that it was used, that it fired." On this same page, page 7, Mr. Filipovic, fifth paragraph, "The men were dressed in civilian clothes. I only saw one man in a camouflage uniform. He had a shirt on his head. He had a classic army cap. So I only saw his eyes. And the cap or the Balaclava was in olive-drab colour, but we didn't use camouflage in practice. We didn't have insignia, considering the differences in caps and so on and so on." Mr. Filipovic, do you want me to read anything else or could I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to this statement, as I managed to count it all, in the area which was commanded by the Patriotic League staff and the Territorial Defence staff, you had all in all 12 companies?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Zecevic, I told you or I quoted you the song about wishes and desires. We -- that these were our plans, and my brother when he was analysing it all, he was doing it with the assumption there would 1200 to 1300 people. These were assumptions, but the actual factual state, as I keep saying to you, has been 700 to 800 people in pieces [As interpreted]. Even in this report it says there were about 800 pieces. And in my testimony, before I even saw this, I keep saying to you, there were about 800 pieces. I say to you there were that many men who were ready to fight, but about a month before the start of aggression against Kljuc, on one of the meetings, when we analysed all this and we were saying, there is this and there is this, I stood up and I said, "The U.S. Sixth fleet won't be able to touch us if we have all these weapons and all these troops." But at the end of the day, it turned out that I was right. Half of these people were only talking and when push came to shove, they fled. So from this last meeting, until the conflict broke out, many of them fled abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, let's go back it to page 6, please, the last paragraph, we just read it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your late brother said, "According to my assessment, we were able to count on, that is I counted on 1200 to 1300 men."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I just told you. He counted on that but the actual situation was not this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you count on something, that means that it really exists. You cannot count on something that doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot break the rules of the Chamber. I could tell you other things. I can tell you about what the Serb side thought but I'm not going to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your late brother Omer, did he tell you about giving a statement in Kljuc in the police station in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned from him, he was arrested on the 29th and the first time I saw him in Stara Gradiska, the 11th of June on the first Hadzijski Bajram, I met him in prison and he then told me that he was being treated rather correctly, mostly thanks to Vinko, who was trying to somehow keep up the old friendship. And he said, "To date, I am alive because of Vinko. But if it was up to Jovo Banjac, I would have been dead on the 29th." And he then told me, "I am being treated as a political prisoner. I am being interrogated. And to date," and this was spoken on the 11th of June, "to date I have not been hit." And he said, "Dear brother, I am very sorry to see what they have done to you." And this is when I found out about it. Of course I didn't know about this. He said he was interrogated. He even said that president Todo Gajic came, and I don't know who else came to interrogate him, to Stara Gradiska, nearly every day, so I don't know specifically because he also told me that in Kljuc, he also gave statements and that he was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam usher, I don't need the document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me here, during your examination-in-chief, you said that you also gave a statement in Manjaca, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you were mistreated before and after you gave the statement, but that in the statement, what's included is what you did say on that occasion, that not all is true but that you did say that on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, during the examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor showed you a document and asked you to comment on the part of that document [In English] 3012, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will try my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember seeing this document, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one thing. During your examination-in-chief, you looked on page 17 of this document, which speaks about detecting and preventing perpetrators of various criminal offences and on that occasion, the Prosecutor stressed this and presented as such that these were isolated criminal offences. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have a reference, please, for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I don't have it over here. I am sure that it was -- may I rephrase, then, the question? Because I don't have unfortunately the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't thought that it would be objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not an objection. I'm simply -- it's the way the question was put so I'd quite like to see what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We all do, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm withdrawing that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, I'm going to read to you the last two sentences of this document on page 17: "So far, up until now, 163 break-ins and 43 incidents of arson have been registered. The intensity of combat activities, the urgency to apprehend extremists, as well as unsafe and dangerous movement in certain areas, has all made the detection of the perpetrators of the aforementioned offences impossible. In addition to that, the complex security situation, the atmosphere of fear and the way of thinking on the part of the citizens who have refused to cooperate, have simply paralysed all our activities." Mr. Filipovic, in your opinion, do you think that 163 break-ins and 43 incidents of arson represent isolated criminal offences or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. This is July, 1992, which means that from the 27th of May until July, 1992, there were many more break-ins and torchings. You can go through the report of the public security station because they were trying to cover themselves because in Kljuc, many buildings were destroyed. You can just go 200 metres near by house and my brother's house and this was all looted, so these two lootings near our house -- excuse me could you please repeat the question so that I can answer it? Was it 163? Is that isolated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 163 break-ins and 43 incidents of arson. Does this represent isolated criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think these are isolated criminal offences. This was done according to plan. This was intentional. How can it be isolated? It's isolated when it's one or two. And I claim there were many more than 163.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to your claim, when you say from the 27th of May to July, 1992, there were many more, you were arrested in -- on the 28th of May, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is not something you know firsthand? You heard about it? You learned about it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not firsthand, but I had the cassette. This was my first touch with the town of Kljuc, with the municipality of Kljuc. So it was from this cassette that I saw and if we could see good recording in the original on that cassette you would be able to count that there were many more than 163, more than 43 incidents of arson. There were not a house that wasn't looted, either television taken, car taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this in relation to the cassette. We wasted sometime in relation to what the cassette showed, in relation to Dr. Kapetanovic. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you said, if I recall well, that he gave a statement and that the following day, he was in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether that was the day after or two days after, very soon afterwards, he was sent to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that in your opinion, this was propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Just like it was propaganda while we were in Manjaca, the Banja Luka television came to film us, camp prisoners, brought in an accordion and for a few cigarettes, they made somebody play harmonica, and then what they say, the footage was here, there are Muslims having a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown P930, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, I will show you a document. Dr. Kapetanovic's name is Emir, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a list of persons from Humic who have not been interrogated, from Plamenica, Velagici to Bocani.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an unofficial document which is a list of people who have not been interrogated and who are supposed to be detained. We can assume that this document comes from the police.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume, when we are talking about people who have not been interrogated from the area of Humic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the penultimate page, you can see a list of the uninterrogated people from Kljuc that are to be detained under item 1. Is the name of Dr. Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Emir Kapetanovic but I don't know whether this is the doctor, but he is this -- it does say Emir Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were there many Emir Kapetanovics in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many Kapetanovics, but I don't know, but I think it is the Emir Kapetanovic because below him there is Husid Raganovi [phoen] and the two of them were brought to Manjaca together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you do think that this is Dr. Kapetanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do think this is Dr. Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it is probably you'll allow for the possibility, that during operative work they came to some information. It was only subsequently that they took a statement from Dr. Kapetanovic and then detained him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot allow for that because the mistake, if that we call the error on the part of the SDS in it relation to Dr. Kapetanovic was that Dr. Kapetanovic had his gynaecological outpatient's clinic in Velagici. So he was accused, there is a document to that effect, he was accused by the public security station. He was accused as being a member of the medical department of the Kljuc Territorial Defence staff, but I'm just saying that his only crime was that he had his outpatient's clinic in the Dom, which is about 3 kilometres from the town because Kljuc was very expensive for renting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dr. Kapetanovic on the 27th of May, 1992, in Velagici, among other things, he also treated Sefik Muratagic who was wounded when the checkpoint in -- the police was attacked in Velagici?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, he said that he was -- up to a point on that day, it was a working day, and he just happened to be in his clinic. He was working. And as far as I know, he wanted, as we say that in Bosnia, when push came to shove, he wanted to split but when there was shooting, they wouldn't -- his people wouldn't let him. They said, "You're the doctor." So he stayed, forced by circumstances. And that's how he administered medical help. If he had known what would happen, of course, he wouldn't have been in Velagici on the 27th of May. Because I know when we called him to join the staff, he didn't want to, because his kum or his best friend, his best man, was Miljenko. He was a vojvoda, or a duke, and he always spoke of, "No, no, I'm with my friend, I'm with my kum. I'm with the duke."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours may I pose one more question and then we can have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we mentioned the videotape that you commented on, do you remember that on one occasion, on the cassette, Mr. Banjac appears on the cassette?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not once, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you commented that when we were watching the tape here, you said that Mr. Banjac was speaking in favour of peaceful movement of people and you characterised this as ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I characterised it, but Mr. Banjac was the one who was doing the speaking, not me. He was talking about the displacement, the movement, the people, and I only said this was ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing. You as a politician, you certainly know, you know, you are aware of Cutilheiro's plan about the cantonisation, Cutilheiro's plan from 1992, about the so-called peaceful displacement or movement of people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know about Cutilheiro's plan from Lisbon, this was not, as far as I know, this was not about moving people, this was just about a division of Bosnia, according to ethnic division, and I know that according to this division, the Muslim side, so to speak, would get -- would have received a lot more than according to the Dayton Agreement. But as for the movement of people, this is the first time that I hear that this plan involved displacement of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the question. I think we should take the break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the break and on that document, I'm delighted that Mr. Zecevic says we can assume it comes from the police because we assume it comes from the police as well, but I should say that it was a document objected to on two grounds. The first, that it was unsigned and unsealed, and secondly, it was actually received by us from AID. So again I'm just making the point, yet again, that on the one hand the Defence object to the authenticity of the document, on the other hand, they are now using them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have stated very clearly that this is unofficial document. When I was asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, with regard to the untranslated document, I have information that the request date was suggested or was put to them as being the end of September and therefore they have been working towards 30/9, that's Monday, deadline. So perhaps Ms. Korner, I mean since the time for your -- for the re-examination of witness I assume would arrive in about two hours' time, if you could do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm going to have the document read through, although it's not the most desirable way of dealing with it, but it's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know, but in the meantime we will have a break of 30 minutes. That should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just one clarification. We have checked out our records. Our records clearly state that we have given this document for translation on the 26th of August, and stated as soon as possible, assuming ten days, because we assumed that this witness will appear of course at the beginning of September. And we in no way suggested the 30th of September because it wouldn't make any sense because at that time we didn't know what was -- what has happened actually, unfortunately, events which took place after the 9th of September, so I just want to clarify that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And [Microphone not activated] Madam Registrar please pass on what Mr. Zecevic has just stated to the CLSS because the two versions are conflicting and we have a right to know. I fully understand of course that the CLSS are very much overloaded with work and I would appreciate their cooperation in this matter to the best of their present capacity and ability. So you may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you anticipate to finish before the next break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Probably not more than 45 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, we were speaking about Cutilheiro's plan. You said you weren't aware of the part that referred to peacefully and moving people out, et cetera, et cetera. Are you aware of the fact that the leaders of the SDA from Bihac, Mr. Ibrahim Ljubijankic Pasic [As interpreted], negotiated on an exchange of population in May and June, 1992? And they were to move Serbs to the Banja Luka area and the Muslims from that area were to be moved to Bihac? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about this. What I do know is that they asked that we be released from Manjaca, they would give people in exchange. They asked for the four of us, four of us Filipovics, they asked for us to be released and they were ready to give as many people as the Serbian side requested. That's what I am aware of. I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that that was as part of an exchange of certain individuals and not as part of an exchange of population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, they asked that we be released, my brother and myself, relative of mine whom we have already mentioned and I don't know who else and they said that in this exchange, they would give the people demanded by the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, have you read Sefer Halilovic's book, "The Cunning Strategy"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm aware of it through the press, but I have not read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic on page 196 of this book, in an extract from the session of the BH Presidency, dated the 20th of June, 1992, discussed that agreement and criticised it. You're not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, if I remember correctly, you testified here that you arrived in Manjaca on the 15th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, tell me, if you can of course, in your opinion, how many detainees were there in Manjaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived there, there were -- I don't know if you have a sketch of Manjaca. I would have brought it with me if I'd known. There are six stables there. When I got there on the 15th of June, there were people from Grapska there, that's near Doboj, people from Kljuc were there and there were people from Sanjani and some others. So in the first three stables, next to the military command, near the offices of Colonel Popovic, that's where there were a few huts in those three -- those three places were full. And in June, when people were brought in from Sanica [As interpreted], and at the time the stable I was in had about 800 plus people, but on average there were between 700 and 1.000 people in the stable. But there were 800 in my stable so 3 times 800 that's 2400, so give or take a certain number, around 2.000, but then when Omarska was shut down, the other three stables were -- people from the other three stables were transferred where the others had been taken, but we had no contact because there was a wire fence separating us, so we had no contact with people over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So around the 15th of June when you arrived there, in your opinion, there were about 2.000 people there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there, there were fewer people, but by the end of June, I would guess that there were about 2.000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It tell me, could you tell us how many guards there were in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could -- I couldn't say, because I was immobile when I got there, but I know that at that time, when we were being taken in, well, I'd say about 50 at least, because above the entrance to the camp there was an observation post, there was a light machine-gun there and there were two soldiers up there. And then a little further on, there were guards who would move around freely, and in this part of the command, there were the soldiers who served there, they had olive drab uniforms and the others were wearing camouflage uniforms. And they had workshops of some sort, they would repair cars. But I don't know. I was immobile. I only went out of my stable on two occasions and went to that part over there. On one occasion, I went to the doctor to be examined and one occasion I went to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in your opinion, about 50 guards?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there could have been more because there were shifts, so perhaps there were 50 of them in one shift and then they would finish and second shift would take over and so on. But there were warnings around the camp, they warned about the mines and you could see how the mines had been dug in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in your statement and some other witnesses also spoke about this, three names were mentioned, a certain Zoka, a certain Spaga and Fadil Bula?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain this to us? Could you -- why only these three names mentioned? Do you know why this is the case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in my opinion, forgive me for this comparison but I know about Your Honours, I know about you, but the Chamber isn't -- the room is full, the courtroom is full. But in the Manjaca camp we knew about Commander Popovic and about the extremists who would beat people to exhaustion, Zoka, Fadil and Spaga, Spaga he was some sort of warden, and he gave himself the right to take a horse and go through the canteen -- let's say it was the canteen. It wasn't really a canteen. It was just a place that had been covered up -- he would go through on horse back and then Tadic -- well, those people persons were mentioned, they were the leading men there. The main men. We called him Fadil Bula, but his name was Zeljko Bulatovic. But because he introduced himself to us and when he beat us he said "I'm a balija like you but I serve Karadzic." He was the most notorious one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you say extremists. You were beaten, when you were being taken into Manjaca, and on that occasion, that person, Fadil Bula he --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I have said. I was first beating in Kljuc and then on the way from Kljuc to Mali Logor and in Stara Gradiska and when I got to Manjaca, Fadil Bula beat me, so that in medical terms, one could say that I was not really a victim in Manjaca. I stand by what I say, but other peoples were victims, but the person responsible for all the evil in Manjaca was Zeljko Bulatovic. He was the initiator. He was the person everyone feared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said that you were only beaten on other occasion after you had been taken in because were you late for the lineup; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said: When I got there for the first time on the 15th, he beat me very badly, and later on, I was beaten when I went to the supervisor. But once they called us to line up -- I think that was every Wednesday or every Tuesday. I can't remember the exact day -- but as I was an invalid, the others knew that you had to go and line up immediately, but by the time I got there I was hit with a truncheon on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, that Bulatovic, Fadil Bula, whatever his name was, on that occasion when you got there, he beat your late brother Omer who wanted to help you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he then found out that you and the late Omer were brothers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we were brothers, yes, because Omer said "I've got to help him. He's my brother." And they said, "Well, since you have to, we will do it to you too." And Omer later told me that was the first time he was beaten, that he hadn't been beaten in Stara Gradiska and he hadn't been beaten in Kljuc either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony you also said that Fadil Bula, this person called Bulatovic, also maltreated your late brother, poured tea over him, mocked him and called him professor, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And similarly, Omer didn't remain in his debt; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Omer was a brave man and he had to have the courage and the daring in a concentration camp such as Manjaca, to reply when he was asked, "What are you thinking about professor?" And he said, "I'm thinking about writing a book." And he asked, "Will there be room for me? He said, "Yes, there will be room for you. You're going to be the main hero in that book, the main protagonist." At that time it was necessary to have the courage to say such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Fadil Bula, Bulatovic had, so to speak, something against your brother?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that is the case. And I think that someone persuaded him to adopt such an attitude because he would suddenly turn up when it wasn't time. When Commander Popovic said, for example, "No one else must enter any more," he would turn up at 8.00 and stand by Omer and then start singing those old Serbian songs. And he would just change one of the words and put the name Omer Filipovic in the song. He would modify the song a bit and provoke him in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Filipovic, the most serious cases of mistreatment in Manjaca took place in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. Mostly after the official command had left, but I personally think that the command couldn't have been aware of this because had I been the commander, when I turned up to work in the morning, I would have asked what had happened while I was absent. And even when my brother was killed, the interrogator - I don't know what his name is - he called me to express his condolences. He said, "Well, this happened while we were not at work. You can see we are trying our best to maintain order when we are here, but we are not in a position to control certain individuals." I don't know the interrogator's name. All I know is that he had a pistol, it wasn't an army pistol, it was some sort of an Colt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told me that as far as you know, the autopsy report after the tragic death of your brother was also incorrect so to say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's my opinion. It says Filipovic Omer there and it says that he died on such and such a day instead of stating that Filipovic Omer was killed, because to die that means when I die a natural death but if someone takes away my life by force, that's murder. And according to the findings of the doctor, when Omer's body in 1998 was exhumed, he determined that Omer had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you were pardoned by the President of Republika Srpska on the 11th of September, 1992. That's document DB97 which I have already shown you. I don't think it's necessary to show you again. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document hasn't been shown to me, but on that day -- well if it's here, I would be grateful if you could show it to me because I have never seen it. But when we set off for England, the investigator who lined us up, literally told us the following: "Thanks to Mr. Karadzic, you are now free men. Mr. Karadzic has signed a pardon for you. Filipovic, you're a little cleverer than the others. Tell them what that means, what a pardon means." I didn't know whether to tell them or not but I said, "Thanks to Mr. Karadzic we ended up in Manjaca." He said, "I didn't ask you about that, but tell them what a pardon means." So I know that for this reason. But I have never seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
