utterances.text: Do Your Honours require me to show the document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness has asked to see it, so I think he's entitled to it. It hasn't actually been shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's show him the -- I don't recall this document ever been shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's never been shown. It's actually also the same as a document which had been marked P422, but I don't know which is the easiest for the registrar to give to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, P422.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible just to make sure that that's the same document? Yes. Yes. Sorry. Put the English version on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen it but these are the people who went to England with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is your name in the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under number 28, it says, "Filipovic, Muhamed." One of the men under number 29 died, I think, Dedic Sefir. When they took us out on the first occasion -- as I said there were no planes -- well, he then died. He died in Manjaca, so he didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. Mr. Filipovic, just a few other questions. I don't want to bring you into a situation in which we would have to talk about something that is not very nice for you, with regard to your late brother, but I would just like to clarify something. Mr. Trbojevic asked you yesterday with reference to your statement the late Omer was buried in the Sehidsko cemetery in Kljuc. Isn't it correct that "Sehid" [phoen] means holy warrior?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Sehid, in our religion, is someone who died while he was on the right path. So translate this however you like, but someone who died on the right path, for a just cause. Since we consider Omer Filipovic, my late brother, to be someone who died for a just cause and a just cause is the defence of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the defence of its people. And given that this is our opinion, Omer Filipovic was buried in that cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I apologise yet again.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just briefly like to remind you of something in the Territorial Defence headquarters, and the patriotic league in Kljuc, you and your late brother Omer, Asim Ibrahim Egerlic, Mr. Avdic and Djeric Nevzad were members of these headquarters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We heard in your testimony yesterday and in the course of these proceedings that Mr. Djeric, Nevzad Djeric, also known as Kedjo was a reserve JNA officer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he was in fact part of your defence preparations of the Territorial Defence in the municipality of Kljuc; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he was an officer. And when I said that Omer joined the reserves on one occasion, Kedjo did too in order to see what was happening. And Kedjo also abandoned the reserves when Seselj was inspecting the troops. He was in Titova Korjenica with his unit and when they lined up, Seselj inspected the troops, Kedjo was revolted and left the line because Seselj was inspecting the troops, so he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me, Mr. Filipovic, that Mr. Djeric, with his knowledge as a reserve officer, helped a lot in organising the Territorial Defence in the territory of the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is certain. He had a -- the rank of a reservist. He was a young man. He was younger than I was. And we could use the knowledge of such people. I don't know what his occupational specialty was exactly. All I know is that he was a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown document DT34, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, I will show you an excerpt from a document published in the magazine called "Ljiljan" on the 23rd of March. There is no mention of the year. As we can see, this was compiled by Nihad Kljucanin. You do know Mr. Nihad Kljucanin, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Lower down, you will see at the end of the document, inside brackets, very small font, you will see information given by Muhamed Filipovic. Before the war Filipovic worked in the municipality of Kljuc as a surveyor. He's a direct witness of the events in Kljuc. He -- the information given he followed from the beginning of 1992 until he was imprisoned on the 27th of May, 1992, and so on. Do you remember that you speak with Mr. Nihad Kljucanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote it from England and sent it by mail. I think that the seat of Ljiljan at the time was in Ljubljana and I explained that according to my recollection, and what people told me while I was a few months in Manjaca, so whatever -- whoever told me what happened and who did what to whom, so I wrote it as a hierarchy, who were the leaders, they were the most responsible. And I can say that everything that happened to us, perhaps we didn't speak about the -- not speaking about the subject of this trial, I can't say Karadzic because Karadzic was not responsible. He didn't kill anyone. That's why I put Jovo Banjac here. He was the head of the municipality. This is the document that I have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the headline it says, "List of war criminals and Chetniks from Kljuc municipality." So that was the subject?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wrote. Somebody called themselves a Chetnik, somebody committed war crimes, somebody withdrew on time, and I know that in 1993, that people said we don't want to be this. So I believe this was written in 1993, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me, under number 51, it said Nevzad, son of Esad, in brackets, Djeric, also known as Kedjo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, why did you include this man that you spoke as one of the organisers of the Territorial Defence in the Kljuc municipality member of the Crisis Staff? Why did you include him and declare him to be a war criminal in -- on 23rd of March, 1993, on this list?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the reason -- he's late now, he's been killed -- he was killed. He crossed over to the side of Fikret Abdic. And he was in Fikret's troops in that region, and he fought against my people, that is his people, and he knew from documents, and it's well known, that Fikret collaborated with Mladic and this other person from Knin, Martic, so if my brother had been in Kedjo's position, I would have called my brother a traitor. I have put Kedjo under number 51 because he, in my opinion, is a traitor. That is my belief. Because a man can do something on one occasion, he may believe that it's correct, and then he would go off his path. He was killed near Kladusa in 1994 or 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. Just a couple more questions. Mr. Filipovic, in the magazine called "Euro Bosna," it's a weekly magazine, and the issue I'm talking about is from March, 1994, in there, you wrote an article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: DT35, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this your article?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was written by my relative, a member of the academy, Professor Muhamed Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour, for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I want to go over some of the things were you asked about yesterday and today. First of all, you were referred to the document P90, and I wonder if you could have that back again, please? This was the announcement, I suppose it is, official statement, of the MBO and the SDA, and it referred in there to instructions signed by Radoslav Brdjanin, and you were asked about that. Now, I'd like you to have a look, please, at the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the contents of this document were not the purpose of my cross-examination. The purpose --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't Mr. Zecevic. It was Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I assumed because I used the document because of the signature. I'm so sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you now have, please, a look at the document -- and I think we will need to put it on the ELMO, Your Honours, because I don't imagine you have it here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not use this document in my cross-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter which of the two used it, one or the other used it and I want to ask something about it. Mr. Trbojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic? Perhaps in the meantime, we can check who used it. I know that it has been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure I used it for the purposes of establishing the signature of the late Omer Filipovic and I never got into the contents of that document. I just stated the name of the document and instructed the witness to take a look at the signature, it at the very end of the document, in order to establish the resemblance of that particular signature and the DT30. And that was all what it was in the cross-examination, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. In fact, it also covers the same topic which was the very first matter that Mr. Trbojevic asked Mr. Filipovic about. It's on page 5 of the LiveNote of yesterday, and the question went as follows: "When you started giving testimony -- on one occasion you said that you had been informed that Mr. Brdjanin, you said he requested a structure of the government in the municipality. Could you explain this it, please, what does it refer to?" And the witness gave an explanation. And this is -- this document refers it to the same set of instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you be given and could we have the English version on the ELMO, P22?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see the Serbo Croat version on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a different document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but perhaps the witness could --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour he hasn't been given P22 yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that but he's put the other document on it and then took away both of them. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He doesn't need the other document any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document dated the 29th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you just move it, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It needs to be turned over to the other side of the page to see the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go then to the front of the page? Sorry, the first side. It's a telegram or telex and it says at the top, "Please deliver this telex to the President of the municipal assembly. Thank you. Order of the SDS Sarajevo, which that was made public at the meeting of the municipal Presidents on the 26th of October, 1991 at 1500 hours in Banja Luka and which was fully accepted at the Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina," and then there is a list of instructions which I'm not going to read through. There is no signature but it has a typed "Coordinator for implementing decisions, Radoslav Brdjanin, vice-president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region." Now, Mr. Filipovic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen it, but in my testimony, it's what I said. Everything that we did according to this, because according to our information, we received that Brdjanin -- we knew that Brdjanin had signed something, and I told this Mr. Zecevic. I know that this had taken place in 1991 and this is saying 29th of October, 1991 and Mr. Zecevic said it was December, but I know that it had taken place beforehand. And on the basis of this document, we reacted and we found -- we heard about this through people talking and telling us some things. I see -- I'm seeing this now for the first time, but this is related to some announcements and all other reactions, because here, from 1 to 14, you can see what had to take place in the new state, how it had to be established, and what we didn't agree with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you made, when that announcement was made by the MBO and the SDA, was it that document that was being referred to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was, I don't know whether there were any other documents that arrived, but in the course of 1991, the announcements that we made I think this related to this one because this is in fact establishment of authority and our reactions related to the establishment of power, of authority, by the SDS, how it was supposed to be done. And because this was in 1991, I believe that our reaction was related to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour I have to object at this time. The witness has just testified that they have never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he had never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That he has never -- well, I assume the MBO and the SDA otherwise he would have seen it. That he hasn't seen that document and that they heard viva voce through somebody about the existence that document so I think that it's improper to be put to the witness that they have done their information from the MBO and SDA based on this document because the witness already said he didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained because basically your question, Ms. Korner, was and when you made -- when that announcement was made by the MBO and the SDA, was it that document that was being referred to? Actually the witness said they were aware that Mr. Brdjanin had signed something but I think the objection is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not proposing to take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I know this is the last day Madam Fauveau and Mr. Zecevic will be here, but I really must object to two counsel from the same team getting much. It's one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection which is a linguistic one which is nothing to do with our client. This document according to what is written in the document, or at least in the translation, is not at all addressed to the President of the municipal assemblies of Krajina. It is actually to the President. I believe it's in singular, to one president. We don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you turn it once more so that we see the front of the document? Here it says in English, "Please deliver this telex to the President of the municipal assembly. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's singular. We cannot conclude that this was to the President of all the municipal assemblies in Krajina. This is in singular.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, it's correctly translated and if I read it out as in the plural, then it's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. You're objection has been sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to change it into the plural?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I just want to explain to Ms. Korner that I am sitting separated from my counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. If Madam Fauveau had taken over from you, I would have stopped her, obviously, but that's why I wanted to first hear what she had to say before I could take a decision. Yes, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all that I want to ask about that document. Thank you very much. You can take that document away. I'd like you to have back, please, the document P1010 that you were being asked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday at page 58 of the LiveNote, were you asked by Mr. Filipovic to look -- I'm sorry, by Mr. Zecevic, to look at that document in relation to the date, on page -- could we have the English on the ELMO? On page 1. It's the beginning of the report, the Crisis Staff that was set up by the executive board of the Kljuc Serbian Democratic Party on the 23rd of December, 1991. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, "Report on the work of the Crisis Staff, War Presidency of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly in the period since 15th of May, 1992," and it says here, "Signed Kljuc".

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, do not worry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27, not December, 29th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you go to the paragraph on the first page of the B/C/S that starts, "The Crisis Staff which was set up by the executive board"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, as Ms. Korner just said, I used it for the purposes of establishing the date only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know you did, and now I'm going to use it for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know you did, but once you opened the door to this document, I'm going to go through the rest of this document, I'm afraid, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we have clearly -- we used ten minutes yesterday to explain our position on that document, why we are objecting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the position, Mr. Zecevic, is this: That once this document has been put to the witness, and therefore has been brought before the Chamber as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we are going to take into consideration every bit of information that it contains. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution did not make use of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was -- I explained yesterday that we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was very simple at the time yesterday, why on earth did the SDS have to, in July of 1992, have to explain that the Crisis Staff was formed on the 26th of December -- 23rd of December of the year before. Yes, but let's hear what the question is, and if it arises out of that document, obviously I have to allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, anyway, we are objecting to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The rule of cross-examination -- of re-examination is that I'm entitled to re-examine on any items that you deal with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. First of all, let's have a look at what the actual -- this document actually says about Crisis Staffs in general. The first -- because it's been put to you that you're mistaken when you say the Crisis Staff was set up before December. It states in paragraph 1, does it not, that the Crisis Staff that was set up by the executive board of the Kljuc Serbian Democratic Party on the 23rd of December, 1991, was expanded at the meeting held on the 14th of May. And it then describes itself as a crisis -- it was transformed into the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. So Mr. Filipovic, do you understand that to mean - whether this is true or not is another matter - but do you understand that to mean that the first Crisis Staff was an SDS one and it then became a Kljuc Municipal Assembly one?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. First there was SDS Crisis Staff but as I said yesterday and before that, this took place before the 23rd of December. The very first document that was handed to me says that it had already existed from before. But first, they were SDS Crisis Staff and then they took over all the competencies of the SDS Crisis Staff and the municipal Crisis Staff as well, and when the war started in May, since we disappeared from Kljuc, they basically took over this as their own right to be War Presidency or war command, civilian command, or whatever, the way they have taken it over, but the way I see it, they took it over. This was the SDS Crisis Staff which then became War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And indeed, if you then move to the fourth paragraph on that page, it says, "The Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly was set up on the 31st of May, 1992, pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia as the War Presidency of the municipal assembly, and as such has carried out to this day, duties which were within the competence of the assembly." Now, it was also suggested to you at one point today that there was a coordinated attack between the Muslim TOs of Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc, to cut off the ARK. Do you remember that suggestion? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic mentioned this. He wanted to prove that we had the intention to cut off the autonomous region, Bosnian Krajina, into two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or to cut up or divide it into two. And I said that we, as people of Kljuc, that we worked on our own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the first question I want to ask you about is that: You have already said there was no coordinated attack and given your reasons. But as far as you were aware, did you have sufficient men or arms to start an attack against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. That's why I wanted Mr. Zecevic to read how many shells we had. With four shells, you can't possibly go into an attack. Four shells, this is just to fire them, to have a kind of show that there is something. But they had everything behind them. They had the support of the JNA, they had a logistics. I said yesterday how come that the Serb side had aircraft, helicopters? I would have all understood all these weapons had it not been for the helicopters; one side can have everything and the other two can't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- you to have a look, please, with us at how the Serbs themselves describe what happened in this document. Page 3 in the English translation, at the second paragraph, begins, "The Crisis Staff (War Presidency) of the assembly based its work and activities on team work. During the period covered by the previous report, the Crisis Staff meetings were held at least twice a week and at the beginning on a daily basis. During the armed conflict, representatives (commanders) of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regularly attended the Crisis Staff and War Presidency meetings. They commanded and carried out the war activities for the defence of the territory and citizens of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly against Muslim extremists. They cooperated and coordinated everything very well with the Crisis Staff. All important and significant issues in the military and police domain were not resolved outside the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to object again, Your Honours, at this time because this was not a part of my cross-examination, neither of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Zecevic, if -- the cross-examination arises out of the -- sorry, the re-examination arises out of the fact that there has been a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that some issues were put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What Ms. Korner is trying to do now, she's picked up one issue, namely your suggestion to the witness that there was coordinated efforts by the Muslims in three municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That there was an attack, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That there was an attack, a coordinated attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness also answered very specifically, that while they had practically nothing to attack with, presumably, as he put it, because there were only four shells by way of ammunition, the other side, the Serbian side, was fully equipped and operational. And the next question that she has just put arises out of that. That is why I stopped -- I did not allow your objection before, and that is why I cannot allow it now. I mean, it's a sequitur, it's a sequence of questions, arising out of a point that you tried to make with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just finish this paragraph? "All important and significant issues in the military and police domain were not resolved outside the Crisis Staff of the municipal assembly. This period could be described as a period of very successful cooperation between the Crisis Staff and military bodies in defeating the armed resistance of Muslim extremists. The Crisis Staff of the municipal assembly has particularly praised and acknowledged the 30th Division of the 1st Corps for the successful action of crushing the resistance of Muslim extremists. After the successful crushing of the resistance of Muslim extremists by the members of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and members of the regular and reserve police forces, as well as the entire Serbian population," I'm going to leave out the rest of the paragraph because it deals with civilians. And at the end of the page, "Despite the results that the army and police achieved in crushing the resistance of Muslim existence (sic) in the territory of the war activities," et cetera -- I'm going to read the next bit to deal with another matter that was put to you. Do you see any reference in that document, Mr. Filipovic, to an attack by the Muslims or any kind of coordinated action between the TOs of Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour has thrown me completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked the witness, "Do you see any reference in that document, Mr. Filipovic, to an attack by the Muslims or any kind of coordinated action between the TOs of Prijedor, Sanski Most and Kljuc?" And then I interrupted you. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't, because there wasn't any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, then you -- it was -- you were asked about a matter that I had raised in examination-in-chief, namely the crimes that were committed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I did find the reference, Your Honour, I may say, and it was, in my view, taken out of context, but nonetheless ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you were asked about that, and I want to look at what they wrote, the Serbs themselves, about these incidents. If we continue with that paragraph, "In the territory where there were war activities, and also on other territories later on, certain negative tendencies appeared which are not characteristic of the dignified Serbian people. To be more precise, paramilitary groups and individuals appeared and carried out robberies, torchings and attacks mostly in villages with the Muslim population, once the combat on mopping-up operations in the area were over. They also broke into houses and moved into abandoned apartments." This is a global description, if-- I suppose one could put it. In your view, is this an accurate or an inaccurate description of what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. For example, I was captured and sent to Manjaca. My wife was forced to Travnik. My house remained there and Serbs moved into it. Everything that I had, all the property that my father had obtained, that became their property. Prior to that, before they gave my wife permission to leave Kljuc, she was asked to sign a declaration, according to which she was giving her property to the Republic of Serbia, to Republika Srpska. My wife refused to do so. She didn't want to sign that. And the same thing happened to all the Muslims and Croats who left, the same thing that happened to me. So when we left, we did not know what was going to happen to our things and to our property. This was plunder. They would reward their fighters who had been to the front and who had excelled themselves. I don't have any proof but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... answered the question enough already. We don't want any repetition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on this document, because you've been asked a number of times about instructions you received from Sarajevo, in the page 4, same page, fourth paragraph, "The Crisis Staff authorised the executive council of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly to consider certain issues and reach decisions which are in its competence." I'll leave out the rest. And then this: "At every meeting the Crisis Staff [War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly] considered the conclusions of the Banja Luka Regional Crisis Staff which were binding as regards all issues connected with life and work in the municipality. Furthermore, the Crisis Staff [War Presidency] of the municipal assembly resolved certain personnel issues in the judicial system, the public prosecutor's office," et cetera, et cetera." And then I don't think we need trouble with the rest of this document. Thank you. Now, you can take that document away. Thank you. Now, finally on this question of the crimes that were you asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may object now, I believe you will sustain my objection now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't heard the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard the question. It was read as a -- my question was instructions from Sarajevo and now we are talking about the instructions of the Crisis Staff from ARK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no question. Ms. Korner went on reading bits and pieces of the paragraph but with no question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours find that appropriate in the re-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I was going to ask Ms. Korner when was she going to pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I stood up earlier than I should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I saw her sit down because you stood up. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was merely drawing the conclusion that the question -- I mean, the questions were put to him about the MBO taking instructions from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I could have asked a question I suppose, does this show that the Kljuc Crisis Staff was taking instructions from the regional Crisis Staff? Answer yes. I decided that wasn't worth it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So next question. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be another question then. How is it that the witness knows this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He knows what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the paragraph which Mrs. Korner read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He doesn't say that he knows anything about it. [Microphone not activated] Ms. Korner read from a document which allegedly is an SDS document. That's it. I mean no question put and that's the end of the story. This Trial Chamber is not going to take any cognizance at all of this last part of the proceedings in which Ms. Korner read from that document with no ultimate -- because you read out -- first you faced the witness with regard to the questions that were put to you with regard --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She read it out very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's it. The document is there. It says what it says, but there is was no question on that relevant part of the document. So -- I mean we don't need Ms. Korner or anyone else to read to us from any particular document which is before us in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine. I know that this is some ongoing saga about whether I can read documents or not but Your Honour said you're not going to take cognizance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This last -- no, the fact that you continued reading from that document. We didn't say that we are not going to take --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Into account the document itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are ignoring the fact that you stood up to re-examine the witness on what he had stated about receiving instructions from Sarajevo. And then was not really followed up by a question. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for once I ignored --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. You have every right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like though to deal still with the question of the crimes that were committed in the area of Kljuc. Could you be shown, please, P1045? And 1046 thereafter? They are roughly the same sorts of document. Could we have the English on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 28th of September, 1992, headed the Public Security Station in Kljuc and it's a report concerning the crimes committed in the municipality area from the start of the armed uprising on the 27th of May. And it begins by stating that, "On the 27th of May, 1992, Muslim extremists incited an armed uprising during which three members of the Serbian military and police were killed and 30 were wounded. An enormous increase in crime followed during the time of combat operations." And then they list the crimes. And they -- they say, "These are indicators that were officially reported and do not show the actual state of affairs since a large number of crimes were not reported due to fear." And then it goes on to deal with break-ins and then "The" start of the war was characterised by break-ins into businesses and illegal entrances by the army into Muslim apartments. "There was a process of provoking fear in exercising pressure on Muslim inhabitants to move out by burning their houses, throwing explosive devices, firing from Zoljas and infantry weapons at apartment buildings." Before your arrest, Mr. Filipovic, had that started?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had. In my testimony, I said that before I was arrested, there were two murders; one in Kljuc and the other in Sanica. And what is further stated in this report, these are events that took place in Kljuc in a period when we Muslims and Croats were practically absent from Kljuc. And the few of us who had remained, the Serbs allowed themselves to turn up in front of their houses and if they decided to do so, they would kill people on the spot. They could kill families. They were known to rape people and what it says in this it police report is correct. What the chief, Vinko Kondic, has stated is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They go on to say it was known to happen that it an entire hamlet of 20 houses Sljivari and Crnalici would be set on fire in a single night. Did you hear about those incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before or after his arrest?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, did you know about -- did it happen before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this happened after the arrest, but I've heard about this too. When they say that things were set on fire, people were put into stable -- into a stable and they set fire to it in the village of Crnalici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, in fairness's sake, I would ask you to go back a little and break down your question pointing -- pinpointing it in time to the period prior to his or until his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And subdividing it into the various activities, murders, fires, explosions, thefts and whatever and then the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- provocation of fear, because I think it's as far as murders are concerned, he did tell us that there were two at least that he could identify before his arrest. But the rest is a little bit hazy and I'm not quite clear in my mind whether everything happened before or after or both before and after so we better --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just break it this down into Filipovic into what's mentioned in that first paragraph? Before your arrest, was there already -- were break ins into businesses and illegal entrances by the army into -- well, let's deal -- I'm sorry. Again it's too many questions. Businesses, had there already been illegal entry into businesses before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There had. Into catering establishments and into private houses too. As proof I could mention my house, my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then just move to the next thing? That they -- the burning of houses and the throwing of explosive devices, et cetera, did that happen before your arrest or did you hear about it subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday we spoke about Pudin Han, but houses weren't burning but hay and stables, that was before I was arrested. And explosive devices, that is to say hand grenades were thrown, that is when the Serbian army was returning from Kupres, because they would spend ten or 20 days at the front, they would then return and as they were returning, they celebrated because they were alive and they would throw explosive devices. They would drink, they would celebrate and throw explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move to the next paragraph on that -- the last paragraph on that page, the most serious of the crimes, murders, began to be committed immediately after war operations. Most often this involved taking persons out of their family homes and killing them in front of the threshold. We stop there. Had anything like that happened before your arrest? Or did that -- was that something you learned about later?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these things later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the murder of -- four monstrous crimes, such as the murder of four Muslims, two killed with a sledge hammer, one had his throat slit. Again was that something you heard about subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A mass murder of 12 persons from Donja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to because he said there were only two murders occurred before his arrest that he could recall, so all the others must be subsequent to his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then go over the page. It's over our page. Can we turn that over on the ELMO? Recently, houses abandoned by Muslims" -- it must be those of Muslim nationality -- "who moved out are being looted on a massive scale." And this report is September. You've told us that your house was looted. When did your wife actually leave?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that my house had been set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, looted. I'm sorry, looted. I thought you told us your house had been looted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was captured on the 28th of May, and on the 1st of October, my wife left Kljuc with our child.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When was your house ransacked, looted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My house was ransacked when I was arrested. Only academic literature was taken away. But my brother's house was looted. Everything was taken, the car, his possessions. But only technical literature had been taken away from my house because my wife was present when they were carrying out the search, and in the course of the search, there was a, let's say, a decent policeman who did his duty and made sure that they behaved correctly. But they only took away the books - I'm a geodesics expert - and they have plans in this field, and the reason for which they took these books away is that I spied, but this was a professional book from -- written by Professor Ilija Zivkovic. It was something I used to study, but this was used as evidence to show that I had acted as a spy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally on this document, this: "Through operative work, we have gathered information that the perpetrators are persons in uniform, that is to say members of the military who are not under the jurisdiction of the public security station. However, due to the war conditions, the military security organs have only seldom discovered the perpetrators and sanctioned such deeds by sending them to the front line. Those crimes -- these crimes are being reported to a station that simply does not know how to deal with them." Now, I am going to ask a question on this, but before I do that, can we just look at the second report which is very similar, dated the same day, which is Exhibit P1046? And if we look at the English version --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, put on the ELMO, 1046. No, 1046. It's a different document. Can we just have the front page, the first page of 1046 put on the ELMO, the English? This one. Oh, God. Sorry, I didn't understand that. Okay. All right. Perhaps I can just deal with it because there is only one line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This slightly expands on the military. "Information collected through intelligence work reveals that the perpetrators were in uniform. That is, they were military persons outside the authority of the SJB. However, because of wartime conditions, military security organs seldom disclosed the identity of perpetrators and punish such acts by sending them to the front line." Now, as far as you were aware -- first of all, before your arrest, were the people who were committing those acts in military uniform or civilians? That you've described to us, that you were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms. But there were comical situations too. For example, they would go to the front in Croatia or Kupres, loot something there, and a soldier who would be in a military uniform, but he would have football boots on, and then we would laugh at him and say, "Look, he went and looted houses and doesn't know what football boots are." He has a remote control for a television, and he would say, "Look, I've brought a TV from the front," but it was a remote control. It wasn't a television. So at the time, we laughed at this, and we said, "Look at these soldiers. They walk down the roads in football boots. Their feet will be full of blisters once they get to Kljuc."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second question is this: Are you aware of anybody who reported the crimes that were described in this document to the SJB at Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm talking about this period, end of May onwards, not before that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of May onwards, I know nothing about that, but according to what people said, I know that people weren't allowed to report this because if they did, and said that, "Person X came and threatened me," then the following day something would happen. So people were afraid, and because of this, they did not report certain events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Filipovic. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Filipovic, that brings us to an end. This is the end of your testimony here in this Tribunal -- in this case, at least. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal. Thank you for having accepted to come over here and give evidence. Again, it has not been easy for you, both because of the circumstances and also because you had to come here, go back and then come back again, knowing that your physical conditions were not -- was not that good. But I can assure you that you will now be given all the attention you require before you return to your country. You may leave the courtroom. You will be escorted out by the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could I just ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission? Would it be possible to have a photocopy of that document in which I was released? Because I am not someone who is afraid and I walk around Banja Luka. Someone might arrest me, and then I'd be able to show this person a document, to prove that -- I can prove that I'm -- in legal terms, I'm released, but some fool could stop me intercept me in Banja Luka and I'd have to go through 1992 once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will make sure Mr. Filipovic gets a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. You will have a copy of that document before you leave this building today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour there is one last thing. None of us -- at least we weren't given copies yesterday of the documents that he brought with him, and I didn't know whether they have been returned to him.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I left a copy with Susan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were given copies, all of us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I left a copy with Susan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I want to know is whether they have been returned to Mr. Filipovic, the originals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received it but I'm asking for what Mr. Zecevic showed me, the document in which I was pardoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I know. You will have a copy of that document before you leave this building, as I told you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a number of administrative matters to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be Your Honour wants to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two options. How long do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've really got to do, as it were, some minor -- major -- some sort of organising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think it's better to have a break and then we come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes exactly. If it was a matter of just a couple of minutes, I would have asked the interpreters to -- and we would have stayed a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it may take a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's more, we will have a break. We will resume at 12.00 -- sorry, at 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, during the break, we managed to get a request in relation to the translation in question. Since the Defence doesn't have the right to contact the CLSS so we asked the Registrar's office, and what was marked on this request was that it was urgent, and then later on, somebody added, end of September. I just wanted to clarify this and present the facts as they are. Another matter that I wanted to address is in relation to the use of the documents contested by the Defence. All the document that is we contested, we still contest them. The fact is, however, that these documents were admitted into the file on the 26th of August so the Defence cannot pretend that they do not exist. We have to use them and to use them for our benefit since we do not know which probative value the Chamber will give them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not start this argument, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I really want to deal some matters of administrative concerning witnesses and the like but it's the consequences of the severance which is effective as of today. The first is this: Your Honours we can, if Your Honours want, produce a new indictment specifying only Brdjanin alone but effectively, other than removing the biographical details of Talic, the indictment will remain the same because the activities ascribed to Talic form part of the joint criminal enterprise so -- but if Your Honours feel you wish to have a new indictment produced, we can do that during the break. That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We reserve our position on that. I don't think on two feet that that should be necessary. It will of course be necessary, I suppose, in the case of General Talic at this point but we will think about it. It has crossed my mind of course and I have been thinking about it but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's just more paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. It doesn't really make a difference at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Although, it's pointed out to me by Ms. Sutherland who is our expert on documentation that when there has been a severance, the number changes slightly and I think -- and I see the Registrar nodding about that, so it may well be simply for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why should it change for Mr. Brdjanin's case and not for Mr. Talic's? This is ongoing and the other one will or will not resume depending on what the future --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I know but -- yes. I think the thing is, though, that you've ordered there to be separate indictments, and therefore, each will have -- it would have the same number, but I think it goes dash 1 or something like that, dash 2. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no qualms with that. I mean if it's for administrative purposes, that's what you would like to have, go ahead. It's no problem with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, can I just ask: Will the indictment against Brdjanin be whatever the number is dash 1?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think I should discuss this with my boss as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Frankly, my preference would be to retain the indictment against Mr. Brdjanin as it is. And then if anything changed that -- for General Talic, the reference number, but as far as this case is concerned, even for -- I don't know. I mean I don't know what the practice of the Registry is but to me it makes more sense once this is the ongoing trial, to retain the reference number or registration number and change the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think maybe we had better discuss -- I'll get somebody from the team it to discuss this with the registry and we will see what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not of that much importance to us. For the records, even later on, if we are going to research something and you research it by case number, or whatever, I mean, why should Mr. Brdjanin's case have two numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, well this is some sort of admin matter that I think somebody will have to sort out, not us, if you see what we mean and we will do whatever is required on producing a new indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that leads to the second matter. Clearly all motions, therefore, when filed will be filed only in the case of Brdjanin. I think that must follow. Thirdly, we propose to stop at this stage any further disclosure to the Talic Defence. Really for two reasons. The first is it's enormously expensive and a huge waste of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's -- one moment. Because as far as the composition of this Trial Chamber is concerned, now I can only pronounce myself on behalf of the other two judges only in so far as Brdjanin's case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think Your Honour is still seized of the Talic matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will have to discuss that with the President.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. It would seem to me exceedingly odd if Your Honours weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is more than that involved. There is also the ad litem Judges involved and there is a practice that we adopt here as to the assignment of cases to ad litem Judges and I don't think the ad litem Judges, the two ad litem Judges I have with me in this case can also be assigned to another case while this one is still going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I'm asking for a decision. I'm just giving you the information so it's clear to all parties. At the moment we are saying we are taking that decision. We are going to stop disclosure to the Talic team for two reasons. One is that it's exceedingly expensive and I don't know which of the team will be where and how we are supposed to reach any of them. Secondly, if there is going to be a trial at any stage of Talic on these matters, we will then, whatever has been disclosed will be disclosed in advance of that with sufficient time so I'm merely for these purposes giving that information to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever you're going to say, Madam Fauveau, is with this reservation, you will not get a yes or a no or any comment from us for the simple reason that until I am given the green light from the President that I am still seized, together with Judge Janu and Judge Taya of the case against Talic, I don't think I can make any pronouncement or comment on what Ms. Korner has just stated. I will allow it for the record but that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this moment, we are not concerned by the disclosure. However, we are concerned by the indictments that will follow the current indictment. In the current indictment, Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic were charged with -- were charged together and this was a joint trial. We for the reasons that are outside of our control, this trial has to be severed so there will be two trials. What we want to avoid is that in the trial against Mr. Brdjanin, that General Talic's name appears and any element of proof against General Talic are introduced into the trial against Mr. Brdjanin. We are the counsel of General Talic and we have a duty and obligation and we have to defend General Talic in all trials in this -- before this Tribunal so it is clear that General Talic doesn't -- obviously he's not going to be found guilty, if his name isn't quoted, but we do not wish him to be declared guilty because he's not here and he's not going to be able to defend himself. General Talic has, like any other person, fundamental right to be considered presumed innocent until found guilty. He also has the right to defend himself. So we are opposed to the only biographical data on General Talic being here. We believe that there should be two separate indictments and General Talic should not be tried in this trial against Mr. Brdjanin, just like Mr. Brdjanin would not and should not be tried in a trial against General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid there is a fundamental misunderstanding there of the legal position. In exactly the same way as Mr. Zupljanin, who has not yet deigned to put in an appearance at the Hague, is being talked about in the trial, so will General Talic, so will other people not actually accused. I'm afraid that is the nature of a joint criminal enterprise. This is not a stand-alone matter against Mr. Brdjanin. Our allegation is that he, General Talic, Mr. Zupljanin and various others were engaged in this conduct, so I'm afraid that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I believe that the position of Mr. Zupljanin is not the same as that of General Talic. Mr. Zupljanin isn't here. He knows very well that he has been indicted, and he's not here. General Talic was here and he has Defence counsel defending him, and General Talic is not here today not because he does not want to be here but because he cannot be here. It is his fundamental right to be here but he cannot be here, and we cannot change anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, this is a purely legal matter which will be dealt with as we go along, but I invite you both to keep the various concepts involved distinct, one from the other, and -- it's something that I am not going to comment on now because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I understand the suggestion being made by Madam Fauveau, it's that when we produce a new indictment, all references to General Talic should be removed. I think that's what she is asking. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, we want all references to General Talic to be taken out of the indictment against Mr. Brdjanin, but again we do not wish to -- for the Prosecutor to show any evidence against General Talic during this trial against Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a ruling because the answer from the Prosecution for legal reasons which I needn't go into is no to both, that the name and all the description of the acts of General Talic will remain and that we will be leading evidence to show, though obviously in less detail, that's what the week is being used for, to show the criminal -- what we allege to be criminal activities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, Ms. Korner and Madam Fauveau, the situation -- I think everything must be put in its proper perspective. As far as I am concerned, there are several issues involved. Number 1, General Talic is no longer a co-accused in this trial. Before me, I have -- before us, we have one trial now involving one accused only, who happens to be accused also of a joint enterprise. Now, having the other parties involved allegedly -- allegedly involved in the joint enterprise as co-accused in the case is relevant. They don't necessarily have to be co-accused in the case or they don't necessarily have to be present in the case to integrate the charge of the -- the charge of joint enterprise. Once there is a joint enterprise, just as in all other cases of complicity, for example, where the accomplices are known or unknown, but if known, are -- have not been found and are not being charged, the situation is very much the same. I don't think you have any further voice in this trial, Madam Fauveau, as Defence counsel for General Talic. You can please in General Talic's case, not in Mr. Brdjanin's case. What I can assure you is that this trial will not come to a conclusion of guilt or otherwise of General Talic because that is no longer an issue. But I don't think you can tie the Prosecution's hands or the Court's hands, if the charge was and is to remain one of a joint enterprise, to have even the name of General Talic and -- removed from the indictment, and if that is not going to be removed from the indictment, and is part of the indictment, then how can you pretend or expect us to stop the Prosecution from bringing forward evidence to show who the other participants in this possible alleged joint enterprise were? He's not the only person who was mentioned. If you look at the indictment, there are several other persons. Forget Zupljanin because Zupljanin perhaps is in a different position than the other persons that are mentioned as having participated in this joint enterprise. But there are other persons. I don't need to mention any one of them. Do you mean to say that the moment a witness takes the stand and mentions Mr. Karadzic or Biljana Plavsic, I say, "No, you have no right to mention those two persons or what they may have been involved in"? Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not about mentioning General Talic's name or the name of Mr. Karadzic or anyone else. Of course I'm talking about the introducing of evidence and looking for possible responsibility of General Talic in the trial against Brdjanin. Obviously, I have nothing to say in the trial against Mr. Brdjanin. I have always, and as long as I am a legal representative of General Talic, I will always defend his interests. What I was saying about references to General Talic in a trial against Brdjanin, I can also turn it around and say, what about references to Mr. Brdjanin in a trial against General Talic? So I'm saying exactly the same things are valid for a trial where Mr. Brdjanin may be mentioned in a trial against General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It's now the trial of Brdjanin and therefore, any applications made by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- position we need to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We don't need to take this any further. Your Honour, then, so as then regards disclosure, I understand from the Defence to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't discuss that because I told you, I don't know what your position with regard to the trial of General Talic is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am merely saying, Your Honour -- I've already said I don't think it's a matter for Your Honour, unless Your Honour, once seized of another case, makes a ruling. I'm just stating the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next thing is witnesses. No, the witness schedule. I think Your Honour has already been given it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were given a sheet of paper this morning with four names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. It's not -- this is only to cover -- we had to do some reorganisations because of all the to-ing and fro-ing and so that's the list and we provided that to the team for Mr. Brdjanin. The -- I want to say something else and I've forgotten what it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean to cover these four in one week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I hope. Your Honour, I'm just checking that. The first three are all -- yes, we anticipate fairly quickly. The last, as you can see, 7.106, he's the one who has been mentioned and he's likely to take a little longer. Can I just have confirmation that the Court maintenance has been moved so we've got the whole week next -- the week of the 6th? I think that's the message I got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will -- I will confirm that to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's only a four-day week? I thought it had been moved you gave me a document that showed it had been moved to a later week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 7th? No, it's -- the week of the 7th we are starting, we are resuming on the 7th of October in the afternoon and we are sitting right through Thursday but Friday in the sheet that I have, that is the latest marked 24th September, it still shows court maintenance and this we are talking about Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was give a sheet yesterday which showed that the Court maintenance for the 7th had been moved to a later date.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Initially the courtroom maintenance was scheduled on the 1st of November and then we moved to the October, but we still --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Backwards. In other words, it went back.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Explain to you why.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will request -- otherwise we will go over almost certainly, and always mindful of the need to save money, I'd request that we try and find a courtroom on the Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we can find a courtroom I'm prepared to work on the 11th, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you could find us a courtroom on that day? But Milosevic has restarted, Martinovic is sitting all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stakic won't be sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Martinovic is sitting all day, perhaps if we could reach an agreement with Martinovic to sit the -- instead of the all day, either the morning or the afternoon session, then we can alternate with them. That is possible. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honour, Ill leave that in Your Honour's hands. The only problem that has arisen and which is unresolved yet, because we haven't had an answer, is that that next week is the week of the Bosnian elections and the elections are actually on the Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next week, this coming week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The week after?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, the week of the 30th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the end of the week is the Bosnian elections. And we are having a problem because I think voting is on Saturday. Therefore the first witness can only be brought up here on a Sunday and we haven't had a response yet from the VWS as to whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long does the voting process take?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no idea, but I think it's a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Saturday, that means 5th October?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, which means that no witness wants to come up on the Friday, which is what normally happens. So, Your Honour, I'm just giving warning. I hope that we'll still be -- manage to get one of the first three witnesses on to a plane on Sunday to be available to testify on Monday afternoon. But if not, we may simply have to deal with the Monday, with the Status Conference that Mr. Ackerman requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me know in that case because I've just turned down an invitation to go to Leiden University on that day at 5.30 because we are sitting for a very important meeting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I understand, Your Honour, will be here tomorrow and next week so we will let Your Honour know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll be here practically all the time so please keep me informed if we are sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We certainly will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, please, should no witness be forthcoming, for Monday, the 7th, we still need to have the Status Conference that we spoke about so the 7th in any case, will be reserved for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I understood, Your Honour, we perhaps will break a little earlier to have the Status Conference, the witness. Your Honour, finally I'm really clearing the decks, as it were, that is, Mr. Ackerman requested that we look or that Your Honours look at the interview that was conducted with Mr. Halilovic and to see whether there was anything that ought to be disclosed as Rule 68. We have had that interview gone through. The case relates to events in 1993 in Mostar. There is only one reference. It was the MBO. We only found one reference to anything to do with arming and that was in general terms. We conclude from that that there is nothing that needs to be disclosed to the Defence on this aspect and we are quite happy to give Your Honours the breakdown, the summary of the even only remotely relevant parts that relate to 1992 if that's requested. And I'm saying that, I know Mr. Ackerman is not here but his co-counsel is and that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless you act upon your own responsibility, Ms. Korner, obviously --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a request from Mr. Ackerman that you, the judges, should examine whether we are correct in this and I'm merely saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put forward the document or whatever you've just suggested for us to be able to take a decision, on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If so required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it would be in the best interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would be able to do that before the -- well before the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll provide a copy today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When we start again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I think that concludes all the administrative matters that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, if there are problems with the -- having the first or any of these witnesses on the 7th, please advise the Defence team even before you tell us. Okay? Because we will be here any way, but they have to prepare for cross-examination and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if there is going to be a variation in the order, presentation of these documents, then the same applies. To us, it doesn't really make a difference because I suppose we will have the statements and we can read them and prepare ourselves but they have to prepare for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honour, I'm not sure -- Your Honour, we are not sure whether you have all the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We might have one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you may have 7.106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm not sure you've got the rest, but we'll check and we will make sure Your Honours get copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You took the hint. So I wish you a happy weekend and a little bit of sun. Thanks, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of my client I have to ask you something. The break that we will have in November, is this a break that we will have for sure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it has been planned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, the idea last time was, if you recall, Ms. Korner stood up and said in the general replanning and rescheduling of the case, perhaps we could reconsider whether we should maintain the ten-day, that's what she said, the ten-day break in November. We will be discussing that and we will come back to you first thing on the 7th of October. In other words, we haven't taken a decision. It depends on what the outlook will be after this Status Conference and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was necessary for our client to know this in order to be able to plan his visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exactly. We will cooperate in that as much as we can. The idea was to stop from the 13th of November right through resuming on the 25th of November. So basically, we were talking of ten, if I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It isn't that, Your Honour -- I simply want to know what visit we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Probably family visits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I remember well in the beginning of the trial, he -- they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Explained that his family comes to visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will cooperate with that. We will not put any obstructions. It shouldn't -- it shouldn't, we will come back, maybe we will curtail the number of days that we had scheduled off, but we will come, we will discuss that. I think first we need to see what the position as far as the remainder of the case is going to be, what is entailed with the reprogramming and -- because I think you have to reorganise the strategy and everything, and also the result of the Status Conference that Mr. Ackerman suggested and with which we agree. And then we take it up from there. I mean we have no interest in taking holidays, I can assure you, except when they are due or overdue. It.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can assure your client that we do keep the -- take these things into account. I thank you. I wish you a nice weekend. And then we will all meet again hopefully on the 7th of October. Thank you.
